slides.title: Buffering
slides.body: Buffering

slides.title: Subheading: Why And What Types
slides.body:
Subheading: Why And What Types
Content:
Buffering temporarily holds data in memory while it moves between a producer and a consumer whose speeds or timing differ, such as a CPU writing to a slow printer or a network card receiving in bursts. Operating systems implement it as one of three schemes, each trading memory for overlap.
Full overlap: double and circular schemes only
Zero overlap: single buffer scheme
Memory cost rises with buffer count used
Scheme choice depends on burst size, steady rate

slides.title: Heading: Single Buffer
slides.body:
Subheading: One Slot Only
Content:
A single buffer offers one memory area between producer and consumer. The producer must wait until the consumer fully drains it before writing again, so production and consumption never proceed together.
Throughput limited by produce-time + consume-time in series
Memory cost: exactly one buffer slot only
Applies to byte-wise devices: keyboard, mouse
No concurrency: zero speed-up over raw transfer

slides.title: Heading: Double Buffering
slides.body:
Subheading: Two Alternating Buffers
Content:
Double buffering uses two buffers so the producer fills one while the consumer drains the other, then the roles swap. This overlap hides most of the mismatch that a single buffer exposes to the caller.
Swap trigger: consumer signals buffer-full completion
Memory cost: twice a single buffer's footprint
Throughput gain: near full producer speed reached
Also known as page flipping in graphics pipelines
Common uses: video frame rendering, audio playback

slides.title: Heading: Caching Vs Buffering
slides.body:
Subheading: Reuse Versus Transit
Content:
Buffering and caching may share the same memory pool but serve different purposes: a buffer holds the only copy of data currently in transit, while a cache holds a duplicate of data that also exists at the source, kept purely to avoid a repeat access.
Invalidation needed when cached source data changes
Buffer freed immediately after single consumer read
OS disk buffer cache serves both transit, reuse roles
Coherency cost: cache correctness versus buffer simplicity

slides.title: Spooling
slides.body: Spooling

slides.title: Heading: Spooling Concept
slides.body:
Subheading: Why It Exists
Content:
Spooling holds an entire output job on disk until a single, non-shareable device is free to consume it. Because the whole job is queued rather than a few bytes, many processes submit work without touching the device directly.
Targets devices only one job can use at a time (printer, tape drive)
SPOOL: Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line
Prevents interleaved, mixed-up output from different jobs
Decouples job submission from job completion

slides.title: Heading: Spooling Concept
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
At a railway reservation counter, passengers drop a filled form into a box and leave, while the clerk processes forms one by one from that box — just as spooling lets a process hand off its whole job to a disk queue and continue without waiting for the device.

slides.title: Heading: Spooling Mechanism
slides.body:
Subheading: Queue And Reservation
Content:
Spooling is built from a dedicated disk area and a controlling spooler process. Each job is written into this area first, then dispatched to the device strictly one at a time in queue order.
Spool directory: disk area holding queued jobs
Spooler process dequeues and dispatches jobs in order
Device reservation: exclusive lock held only for the running job, released on completion or abort
Completed job entry removed from spool after output

slides.title: Heading: Printer Spooling
slides.body:
Subheading: Queue In Practice
Content:
Print spooling is the everyday example: several users send documents while only one printer exists. Each submission becomes a queued job, letting a user continue working immediately instead of waiting at the device.
Each job gets an identifier and a queue position
Administrator can view, reorder or cancel queued jobs
Urgent or small jobs may be prioritised ahead of others
OS print spooler service manages job order and dispatch

slides.title: Disk Structure
slides.body: Disk Structure

slides.title: Heading: Disk Structure
slides.body:
Subheading: Physical Components
Content:
A hard disk drive organises its storage into nested physical divisions that together give the disk its addressing geometry. Four structures define this layout, moving from the storage medium down to the addressable unit.
Platters: rigid magnetic disks stacked on a spindle
Tracks: concentric circular paths on each surface
Sectors: fixed-size arcs dividing every track
Cylinders: same-numbered track aligned across all platters

slides.title: Heading: Platters And Tracks
slides.body:
Subheading: Surfaces And Rings
Content:
Each platter is a rigid, magnetically coated disk with both faces usable, so several platters stacked on one spindle multiply the surfaces available. Every surface is ruled into tracks — narrow concentric rings holding data along circular paths.
Track 0 is the outermost ring, highest number nearest spindle
Track density (tracks per inch) sets storage capacity
Each surface needs its own read-write head
Modern drives pack thousands of tracks per surface

slides.body:
Track Subdivisions
Subheading: Track Subdivisions
Content:
A track is too large to read or write economically as one piece, so each track is split into sectors — the smallest unit the disk electronics transfer in a single operation. Locating a sector historically needed three coordinates together.
Legacy sector size: 512 bytes per sector
Advanced Format (modern) sector size: 4096 bytes
CHS addressing: cylinder, head and sector numbers together
Sectors per track vary by zone; outer tracks hold more

slides.title: Heading: Cylinders Explained
slides.body:
Subheading: Aligned Track Set
Content:
A cylinder is not a separate physical part but a logical grouping: the same-numbered track on every platter surface, stacked one above another since all heads share one arm. Reading within a cylinder needs no arm movement, only a head switch.
Cylinder count on a drive equals tracks per surface
Data spread across a cylinder before the arm moves
Sequential access within a cylinder minimises seek delay

Content:

slides.title: Disk Performance
slides.body: Disk Performance

slides.title: Heading: Disk Performance Factors
slides.body:
Subheading: Three Time Components
Content:
Every disk access takes measurable time before data reaches memory, built from three sequential delays. Seek time and rotational latency come from the disk's mechanical structure, while transfer time is the actual data movement.
Seek time: arm moves to correct cylinder
Rotational latency: platter spins to target sector
Transfer time: data moves across head to memory
Values reported are typically random-access averages
Three Time Components
Disk Performance Factors

slides.title: Heading: Disk Performance Factors
slides.body:
Subheading: Three Time Components
Content:
Every disk access takes measurable time before data reaches memory, built from three sequential delays. Seek time and rotational latency come from the disk's mechanical structure, while transfer time is the actual data movement.
Seek time: arm moves to correct cylinder
Rotational latency: platter spins to target sector
Transfer time: data moves across head to memory
Values reported are typically random-access averages

slides.title: Heading: Seek Time
slides.body:
Head Movement Delay
Subheading: Head Movement Delay
Content:
Seek time is the delay while the actuator arm moves the head to the cylinder holding the target track, growing with distance travelled. Drives publish only an average value from many random-access seeks.
Phases: acceleration, constant travel, deceleration
Minimum: adjacent-track seek, near zero
Maximum: full-stroke seek across all cylinders
Usually the largest share of access time
Seek Time
Seek time is the delay while the actuator arm moves the head to the cylinder holding the target track, growing with distance travelled. Drives publish only an average value from many random-access seeks.

slides.title: Heading: Seek Time
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
An autorickshaw's travel time between two addresses depends on distance, not a fixed fare — just as seek time depends on cylinders crossed to reach the target track.

slides.title: Heading: Rotational Latency
slides.body:
Subheading: Spin Wait Time
Content:
Rotational latency is the wait for platter spin to bring the target sector under the head, after the arm reaches the correct cylinder. It depends only on spindle speed.
Average latency = half of one rotation
Common speeds: 5400, 7200, 10000, 15000 RPM
Worst case latency: nearly a full rotation

slides.title: Heading: Rotational Latency
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A merry-go-round rider must wait for the horse to swing back to the boarding point — just as rotational latency is the wait for the sector to spin back under the head.

slides.title: Heading: Total Access Time
slides.body:
Subheading: Worked Calculation
Content:
Transfer time is the duration to move data once positioning is complete, found by dividing bytes transferred by the drive's data transfer rate. Total disk access time sums seek time, rotational latency and transfer time.

slides.title: Heading: Improving Disk Speed
slides.body:
Subheading: Where Time Goes
Content:
Seek time usually dominates total access time for random workloads, followed by rotational latency; transfer time is smallest for a single sector. Reducing seek distance or raising rotational speed improves throughput more than optimising transfer alone.
Sequential access avoids repeated long seeks
Higher RPM cuts latency, raises power and noise
Disk scheduling algorithms shorten average seek distance
Solid-state drives have no seek or rotational delay

slides.body: Disk Organization

slides.title: Heading: Disk Organization
slides.body:
Subheading: Formatting And Addressing
Content:
A raw disk drive is unusable until it is organized. Disk organization spans two independent layers: preparing the disk physically to hold data, and giving software a way to locate any sector on it.
Low-level formatting: prepares raw platters for storage
High-level formatting: builds file system structures
CHS addressing: cylinder-head-sector triplet, legacy scheme
LBA addressing: single linear sector number, current

slides.title: Heading: Disk Organization
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: Low-Level Formatting
slides.body:
Subheading: Physical Preparation
Content:
Low-level formatting, usually done once at the factory, writes header, gap and error-correcting data onto every sector, preparing raw platters before data can be stored.
Marks sector/track boundaries with header data
Adds error-correcting code (ECC) per sector
Sector sparing remaps a bad sector to spare
Sector slipping shifts later sectors past a bad one

slides.title: Heading: Low-Level Formatting
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A survey team marks numbered plots with boundary pillars before land can be sold — just as low-level formatting marks sector boundaries before data can be written.

slides.title: Heading: High-Level Formatting
slides.body:
Subheading: Logical Preparation
Content:
High-level (logical) formatting builds the structures an operating system needs on top of already low-level-formatted sectors. Unlike the physical step, it can be redone anytime without re-preparing the platters.
Boot sector and partition table written at volume start
File-system metadata created: root directory, allocation structures
Sectors grouped into clusters, the OS allocation unit
Quick format rewrites metadata only; full format also verifies sectors

slides.title: Heading: Logical Block Addressing
slides.body:
Subheading: Linear Sector Numbering
Content:
CHS addressing tied software to a drive's exact geometry, capping capacity as drives grew larger. Logical Block Addressing (LBA) replaces that triplet with one sequential sector number.
Sectors numbered 0 to total sectors minus one
Firmware translates LBA to physical location internally
Independent of actual cylinder, head or sector counts
Used by SATA, SSD and NVMe interfaces today

slides.title: Heading: Logical Block Addressing
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A bank account number identifies an account directly, without stating its branch, ledger and page separately — just as LBA gives each sector one direct number instead of a cylinder-head-sector triplet.

slides.title: Heading: CHS Vs LBA
slides.body:
Subheading: Addressing Compared
Content:
Both schemes ultimately let firmware locate a physical sector, but they differ in what software must know beforehand and how far capacity can scale.
